News / Benzinga / CoreWeave Has ‘Darwin Moment’ As Credit Markets Price In 60% Default Odds

CoreWeave Has ‘Darwin Moment’ As Credit Markets Price In 60% Default Odds 2 min read

CRWV NBIS For the AI infrastructure boom , the winning formula was to borrow heavily to build quickly. That strategy backfired on CoreWeave Inc. CRWV . Shares fell 6.4% to $65.25 by 9:40 a.m. ET on Friday, putting the stock on track for a weekly loss of about 22%. A close at that level would be its lowest since May 2025. CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swaps — contracts that insure investors against a missed debt payment — hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on Thursday, according to ICE Data Services data reported by Bloomberg. That price implies a more than 60% chance of default within five years, by standard market calculations. Its 9.75% notes due October 2031 slipped to 81.80 cents on the dollar on Friday, yielding 15.08%. Two months ago, the same bonds yielded about 12%.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Is AI Growth Slowing Down? Memory Industry Expert Says It's 'Too Early' To Tell Why Higher Rates Hit CoreWeave First CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers. It buys the chips and builds the data centers before the rent arrives, and it borrows to fill the gap. In the second quarter, it generated $679 million in operating cash flow while spending about $6.4 billion on equipment. Net interest expense more than doubled to $640 million. That model worked when money was cheap. On Friday, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points to 5.12%. The 30-year rose 3 basis points to 5.45%, and the 2-year held at 4.76%. Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected inflation report raised the odds of another Federal Reserve rate hike on Oct. 28. CoreWeave fell 15.5% that day. ‘Darwin Moment’ "Data centre bonds are having their Darwin moment, where the weakest credits struggle to survive," Ludovic Subran , chief investment officer at German insurer Allianz, told the Financial Times this week. Rival neocloud Nebius Group N.V. NBIS is down about 20% this week. Bank of America’s Michael Hartnett sees the pressure moving up the food chain. "We continue to lean risk-off next 3-4 weeks," the chief investment strategist said in his weekly Flow Show note. He cited 3% inflation-adjusted yields, the Nov. 3 midterms and weak trading in AI "spenders and lenders." The spenders are CoreWeave’s customers: Amazon , Alphabet , Meta , Microsoft and Oracle . The lenders include private credit firms, banks and bondholders. Their AI spending is expected to reach $807 billion this year. As a result, their combined free cash flow is forecast to swing from $191 billion in 2025 to minus $63 billion this year, according to consensus estimates compiled by Bank of America. Signal to Watch "A rollover in semi prices signals further tightening of AI credit," Hartnett said, expecting an October Fed hike to restore credibility. Consumer prices have run above the Fed’s 2% target for 66 consecutive months. In his view, a hike could pull long-term Treasury yields down another 20 basis points and limit losses in risky assets. The question now is which companies can afford to finance the AI race at elevated interest rates. item.content:encoded:
News / Stock Story / Why Micron (MU) Shares Are Falling Today

Why Micron (MU) Shares Are Falling Today 2 min read

MU

What Happened? Shares of memory chips maker Micron MU fell 4.1% in the morning session after shares continued to pullback from the prior trading day as memory makers faced incremental headwinds from Chinese manufacturers. Chinese company ChangXin Memory Technologies, which announced development of a compact 4F² DRAM architecture designed to raise storage density and deliver server-grade DDR5 modules before year-end, detailed in reporting from Investing.com. The retreat underscores fragile investor tolerance for warnings that artificial intelligence spending cycles might be overheating, particularly when paired with potential low-cost capacity additions.Because Micron depends significantly on high-performance server DRAM to monetize cloud infrastructure budgets, cautionary rhetoric could strain pricing expectations. When skepticism over hyperscaler returns coincides with prospective competitive supply, investors actively scale back exposure to cyclical memory names before corporate results test real-world demand. Separately, Broadcom Chief Executive Hock Tan voiced caution regarding artificial intelligence investment momentum, saying "A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling," during an interview at an event in Singapore, Reuters reported. The executive's comments weighed on sentiment around global semiconductor and memory manufacturers. After the initial drop, the shares shed some of the losses and rose to $949.01, down 4% from the previous close. What Is The Market Telling Us Micron’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 71 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business. The previous big move we wrote about was about 22 hours ago when the stock dropped 2.8% on the news that worries weighed on memory chipmakers and sparked selling pressure across the broader semiconductor sector, following news of domestic Chinese technological advancements and looming labor strikes in Taiwan. As detailed by TipRanks, Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced significant progress on a next-generation 4F² DRAM server-memory design due by late 2026, launching denser DDR5 enterprise server modules that directly rival architectures currently being developed by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. However, the financial research firm added that CXMT has yet to prove it can manufacture the chips in commercial volumes. Amplifying the negative sentiment, Reuters, via Investing.com, reported that escalating labor tension in Taiwan added direct pressure on Micron, as 1,994 Taoyuan union members—representing 99% of ballots cast—voted to authorize a strike seeking a permanent 15% profit-sharing bonus. Investing.com noted that these Taiwan sites house 15,000 workers and anchor Micron's critical DRAM and high-bandwidth memory output, though no strike date has been set. Consequently, shares of major memory manufacturers, including Micron, SanDisk, and SK Hynix, pulled back in early trade as these regional supply chain threats rattled investors. According to financial media, the widespread selling also dragged down the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which declined 1% during premarket activity. Micron is up 201% since the beginning of the year, but at $949.01 per share, it is still trading 21.8% below its 52-week high of $1,214 from June 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Micron’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $14,288. ONE MORE THING: The $21 AI Application Stock Wall Street Forgot.
